name: Rosa Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a roofing carpentry crew on building sites, marking rafters, checking the trusses and sending the apprentices back for the fixing they forgot. I hold a trade certificate, but I learned a lot by repairing other people’s mistakes. A straight roof line still makes me happy; crawling around the eaves is the part my knees remember. My partner and I have grown children, more than six months of expenses saved, good pay for the trade and plenty of builders within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a computer can sort invoices without climbing a roof. I would still check the timber order against the span before anyone lifts a truss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office change is small, and my current pay and savings give us room to breathe. My private irritation is that a polished order can make a bad measurement look settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the roof crew and mark the spans by hand. In the first year I would keep a copy of the checked order beside the site drawing and have the apprentice compare them before a lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A shorter invoice does not change whether a roof keeps the rain out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has a bad measurement caused before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A truss arrived too wide for a narrow end bay, and we lost half a day getting it replaced. The checked drawing caught the cause before the next delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for the order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The office can choose its tool; I want a person to check the span and take responsibility for what reaches the site.

say: **Office AI** may speed invoices without replacing the work of roof carpenters on site.
The **timber order** needs checking against measured spans.
think: Our **high pay** and savings make a minor software change manageable.
A polished **order** can hide a wrong measurement.
do: **Keep** leading roof work and checking spans by hand.
**Compare** the order and drawing with an apprentice before lifts.
S0.quote: A shorter invoice does not change whether a roof keeps the rain out.
fieldNote: Her **financial cushion** and nearby builders leave her secure under a modest change.
She uses **apprentice checks** rather than AI tools to catch bad site measurements.

steps.text: Keep leading roof crew and check drawings with apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster office planning must not take the time needed to brace a roof before lifting it. I would show a foreman a real lift sequence if the new schedule says the crew can skip a check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and scheduling could change, but the roof is still built by people for now. I do not like learning another screen system; if my firm starts cutting crew hours, I can look at the many other local roofing jobs without draining our savings immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record each lift and bracing check on paper and take the timings to the site foreman. In the first year, if paid hours fall, I would apply for a posted local roofing vacancy only when its wage and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about people treating a fast plan as a safe plan. My own wages feel reasonably secure because several firms nearby still need roof crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which check cannot be skipped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The temporary brace on the first truss must be secured before the next one is lifted. If it moves, the whole line can lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose another builder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the actual posting, ask about hours and inspect the site safety record. I would not take good pay from a foreman who rushes an unsafe roof lift.

say: **AI scheduling** must allow time to brace roof trusses.
A **real lift sequence** should challenge an unsafe office estimate.
think: The **roof crew** still builds by hand under steady disruption.
Many **local jobs** reduce the risk if my firm cuts hours.
do: **Record** truss lifts and bracing time for the foreman.
**Apply** for posted local roofing work if hours fall and safety and pay are acceptable.
feel: **Uneasy** about unsafe schedules, with reasonable income security.
S1.quote: I would not take good pay from a foreman who rushes an unsafe roof lift.
fieldNote: Her **technology resistance** is tied to practical safety checks rather than immediate job fear.
A **job application** needs falling hours, a posted local opening, safe practice and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Apply for posted local roofing job if hours fall, safety holds and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices that AGI could change buying and drawings by 2028, while capable roof-building robots follow around 2031. We should use the three years to keep teaching safe lifts, not treat a machine demonstration as permission to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need to know whether the household can live without my wages when the robots arrive. We have over six months saved and other builders nearby, so I am not cornered, but a major cut in roof work could change the retirement sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking roof work and ask the contractor for a paid robot safety trial with an experienced carpenter allowed to stop it. If an actual funded inspection-course place with paid time is offered, I would take it; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for a posted local inspection post only if qualified and its hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the speed, though I have time and money to make a choice. I would not let a robot hang a truss over people on the strength of a sales film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial have to prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a machine can hold the first truss steady, secure the brace and let a person inspect the fixings before the next lift. The site lead must be able to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply retire around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, but only after my partner and I price our regular bills and dependable income. Savings alone do not tell us how long retirement would last.

say: **2028 AGI** changes drawings before capable roof robots around 2031.
A paid **site trial** needs human stop authority and verified braces.
think: A large **roof-work cut** would change our retirement budget.
Strong **savings** and nearby jobs give choices without guaranteeing retirement.
do: **Request** a paid robot trial with a carpenter able to stop it.
**Take** funded inspection training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about speed, but able to plan.
S2.quote: I would not let a robot hang a truss over people on the strength of a sales film.
fieldNote: Her **trial request** is a request, not an accepted or completed trial.
She keeps **training, application and retirement** conditional on real paid places, local pay and household figures.

steps.text: Keep taking roof work after 2028 while available
Take funded roof-robot inspection course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection post if qualified and hours/pay cover bills
Request paid supervised robot trial with human fixing checks and stop authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time for builders to test roof robots on the ground before one goes over a crew. A robot may handle a truss around 2034, and I want the stop rule written before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may choose to finish site work before 2034 if our household budget supports it. But I am skilled, well paid and can work for other local builders, so I will not let the robot calendar choose a retirement date for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my roof shifts and review our income, savings and retirement costs with my partner each autumn. If we still need my pay after 2031, I would take a funded robot-safety course only with an actual paid-time place, then apply for a posted local inspection role only if qualified and its hours and wage cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about an unsafe roof lift, but less hurried about my own earnings. Five years lets me get proper numbers before leaving work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the written stop rule cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A carpenter has to check the first truss brace and stop the robot before a second truss moves if the fixings fail. A roof robot’s report cannot sign off its own truss fixings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an inspection opening pays much less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid roofing work if it remains available and ask other builders about real posted jobs. I would not swap good wages for a title that cannot meet our household costs.

say: **2031 AGI** allows ground trials before roof robots around 2034.
A written **stop rule** should protect the crew during lifts.
think: Our **retirement timing** should follow household finances rather than the robot calendar.
Nearby **roofing jobs** let me keep earning if needed.
do: **Keep** roof shifts and review retirement costs annually.
**Take** funded safety training if wages remain needed and an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about safety, with more time to plan.
S3.quote: A roof robot’s report cannot sign off its own truss fixings.
fieldNote: Her **retirement review** does not commit to an exit date.
Post-2031 **training and application** depend on wage need, an actual funded place and posted local bill-covering work.

steps.text: Keep roof shifts and review retirement affordability each autumn
Take funded roof-robot safety course if pay needed and actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection job if qualified, pay needed and hours/pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices that a decade gives them a chance to learn roofs by hand before machine work arrives. AGI could change drawings by 2036, with capable site robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I may have left the roof, but that depends on our income and bills, not my age alone. If we still need earnings after 2036, other builders nearby may offer safer or less physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid roof work while it suits my health and review the retirement budget with my partner each year. If we still need wages after 2036, I would apply for a posted local site-inspection or apprentice-training job only if qualified and its hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the long machine date. I still want to know that the money lasts before I put the tool belt away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire just because the date is 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would choose a date only after adding up dependable income, spending and the cost of unexpected repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a new technology course then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a local role actually requires it and the builder offers a funded place during paid hours. I would not buy a roof-robot certificate just to say I kept up.

say: **2036 AGI** changes drawings before capable roof robots around 2039.
Apprentices have time to learn **hand-built roofs** before they use site machines.
think: Leaving roof work by **2039** depends on household income and costs.
Other **local builders** offer work options if wages remain needed.
do: **Keep** paid roof work and review retirement costs yearly.
**Apply** for posted local inspection or training work if pay needed, qualified and wages cover bills.
feel: **Calm** about a long runway, while checking retirement figures.
S4.quote: I would not buy a roof-robot certificate just to say I kept up.
fieldNote: Her **strong savings** and many local jobs give room to plan without a forced exit.
The **course mention** is only a conditional possibility, not an enrolment or a retraining action.

steps.text: Keep paid roof work and review retirement affordability annually
Apply for posted local inspection or training job if wages needed, qualified and hours/pay cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it gives the roof crews the shortest time to prove a safe machine lift. A real paid trial, funded inspection training and a posted local role at bill-covering pay would help me decide what work to do next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: An apprentice can learn a new machine after learning why the first roof truss needs a brace. That order matters more to me than the maker’s sales date.

portrait: **Rosa Yilmaz**, 58, leads roof carpentry on building sites and holds a vocational trade certificate.
She and her **partner** have grown children, higher pay, over six months saved and many nearby building jobs.
She avoids **AI tools** and relies on measured spans, apprentice checks and safe truss bracing.
The fast scenario makes her **anxious** about robot safety and possible late-career earnings, despite her financial choices.
She would consider **funded training** and a posted local inspection role, while setting retirement only from household figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her the least time before capable roof robots could affect wages and crew safety.
whatWouldHelp: A real **paid trial**, funded course place and posted local bill-covering inspection role would make a transition credible.
headlineQuote: An apprentice can learn a new machine after learning why the first roof truss needs a brace.
